preamble: A diphthong with a rounded back nucleus and a front offglide ([ɔːi], [ɔɪ]) becomes the plain open-mid vowel [ɔ] when the offglide is lost and the nucleus is kept. Ancient Greek long ωι [ɔːi] (dative -ῳ) lost its offglide during the classical and Hellenistic periods, so that from about the 1st century BC it was pronounced like plain ω [ɔː]. In advanced Southern American English /ɔɪ/ loses its glide, above all before /l/, so that boils approaches balls.

examples.to: Hellenistic Greek τῷ with plain ω [ɔː], the iota no longer pronounced
Hellenistic Greek final ῳ pronounced as plain ω [ɔː]
Hellenistic Greek initial ᾠ pronounced as plain ω [ɔː], later written with iota subscript
examples.note: The long diphthongs ᾳ, ῃ, ῳ lost their offglide from the classical period onwards. From about the 1st century BC they were no longer distinguished from ᾱ, η, ω, and medieval scribes wrote the silent iota as a subscript. Wiktionary's period transcriptions go from Attic /ɔːi̯/ straight to 1st-century CE /o/, after the later merger of ω with ο (ɔ → o).

examples.to: [bɔːlz], close to British or New York balls
examples.note: The from-form is the conservative pronunciation. Part of the Back Upglide Shift: /ɔɪ/ loses its glide and becomes [ɔ], particularly before /l/.
Cajun English shows glide weakening in all gliding vowels, including /ɔɪ/.

sources: Allen, W. S. (1987). Vox Graeca: The Pronunciation of Classical Greek (3rd ed.). Cambridge University Press. https://www.cambridge.org/9780521335553
Labov, W., Ash, S. & Boberg, C. (2006). The Atlas of North American English. De Gruyter. https://doi.org/10.1515/9783110167467
